label: Afternoon edition
summary: Keanu, **the Nasdaq fell 2.6 percent, its worst day since June**, as fears about funding the AI buildout met an oil spike (CNBC, Bloomberg, NBC News). Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said neocloud demand is huge but capital is scarce, and CoreWeave dropped about 10 percent (CNBC). Brent crude rose about 4 percent to $113.17 after the New York Times reported that **the U.S. and Israel are planning new Iran strikes** after the Nov. 3 midterms (NPR, CNBC, Fox News). Iran says seven tankers were hit in the Strait of Hormuz, and Washington pulled non-emergency staff from Saudi Arabia (NBC News, CNN). At home, **California is fighting a Justice Department bid** to set aside ballots from about 20,000 flagged voters, with no ruling yet (CalMatters, Fox News). Democrats sued the administration over what they call prosecution threats against election officials, which the White House calls lawful (Axios, The Hill). Fox News has Trump's approval at a record-low 36 percent and Democrats up 54 to 45 on the House ballot (Fox News). Putin agreed in principle to resume three-way Ukraine talks, possibly around Nov. 10 (Axios). Jobless claims stayed near record lows at 194,000, and the **10-year yield slipped below 5 percent** (CNBC). In science, a Copenhagen model says Earth and Mars were **built in different ways** (Space.com).

alerts.text: Alphabet and Microsoft report earnings Oct. 28 after the close and Amazon follows Oct. 29, and all three fell 2 to 5 percent today.
The DOJ's emergency bid to stop California counting ballots from 20,000 flagged voters is pending, and early voting in Alameda County starts Oct. 24.
NPR and CNBC report the U.S. and Israel are planning Iran strikes after Nov. 3, which sent Brent to $113.
Your watchlist took a hit today: Amazon fell 4.57 percent, Nvidia 4.40 percent and Alphabet 3.15 percent, while Apple rose 1.23 percent.

The 10-year yield fell below 5 percent as investors sought safety, and Brent hit its highest since May 4 (CNBC). Bitcoin slipped 3.27 percent to $81,277.

stories.title: Democrats sue the Trump administration over pressure on state election officials
stories.summary: Democratic leaders say DOJ and DHS threats of prosecution are intimidating election officials; the White House says its actions are lawful.
story: Democratic groups and leaders sued the Trump administration in federal court in Washington on Oct. 21, saying federal officials are pressuring states over voter rolls and threatening election officials with prosecution ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms (Axios, The Hill). The plaintiffs include the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries and a voter. The defendants are Trump, the Justice and Homeland Security departments and their heads.

The complaint argues that threats of criminal charges and even prison time for officials who refuse to comply violate Section 11(b) of the Voting Rights Act (The Hill). It points to Nevada, where DHS first said it had found nearly 16,000 noncitizens on the rolls, then cut the figure to 185, and Nevada officials said all 185 appeared to be citizens. It also cites an Oct. 13 DOJ demand that California set aside ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters the department suspects are noncitizens.

The White House says it is taking "decisive lawful action to protect our elections" and DOJ says its actions are lawful (Axios). Fox News and the Washington Examiner cover the push as enforcement of voter-list laws, and note DOJ has charged 28 green card holders in California. Independent reviews and audits have found no evidence of widespread voter fraud, according to the reporting.

A federal judge in California has also blocked certain DHS noncitizen-voting investigations, finding the methods likely violated the law because of unreliable source data (Fox News). The new suit asks a judge to declare the administration's actions unlawful and block further interference.
stories.flag: No ruling in the new suit had been reported at the time of writing.
facts: The suit was filed in federal court in Washington, D.C.
Plaintiffs include the DCCC, Schumer and Jeffries.
It claims violations of Section 11(b) of the Voting Rights Act.
Nevada's DHS-flagged count fell from nearly 16,000 to 185, and officials there say all 185 appeared to be citizens.
DOJ asked California on Oct. 13 to set aside ballots from more than 20,000 voters.
The White House calls its actions lawful.
stories.left: Democrats argue that the federal government is using its prosecutors as a pressure tool on the people who run elections. The Nevada numbers, they say, show how unreliable the federal lists are: a claim of nearly 16,000 shrank to 185, and those 185 looked like citizens. They see a pattern in which weak data is used to threaten state officials weeks before voting ends, and they say courts exist to stop exactly that kind of coercion.
stories.right: Conservatives argue that only citizens may vote in federal elections and that the Justice Department has a duty to enforce voter-list maintenance laws. They point to charges against 28 green card holders in California and to New Jersey's disclosure that a software error added about 6,600 noncitizens to its rolls as proof that the problem is real. In this view, states that refuse to check federal lists are the ones making election integrity partisan.
stories.next: Watch for a judge's response to the suit and for the ruling on DOJ's emergency motion in California before Nov. 3.

stories.title: White House staff brace for post-midterm fallout after a press secretary lasts five days
stories.summary: CNN reports aides fear a post-election purge, while the White House calls it baseless speculation.
story: Katie Zacharia is out as White House press secretary after about five days on the job, NBC News and Fox News reported. NBC said her first briefing was poorly received and questions arose about her legal background, reporting she had presented herself as a lawyer but did not pass her bar exam. A senior official told NBC she is moving to a new role to be announced later. NBC's sources said a replacement is unlikely soon.

CNN reported on Oct. 20 that administration officials increasingly expect major personnel changes if Republicans take steep losses on Nov. 3, with Trump looking for people to blame. One adviser told CNN, "If we lose both the House and the Senate, there's really no telling what happens." Many aides think the House is likely lost, while advisers still think the Senate can be held. White House spokesman Davis Ingle called the internal-dynamics reporting "baseless speculation."

Chief of staff Susie Wiles is at the center of the talk. Trump said there is "zero chance" he will replace her and called her "smart" and "tough." Former chief of staff Mick Mulvaney predicts she will leave after the midterms, though not because she has fallen from favor (The Hill). Politico corrected a report on Wiles's role in Zacharia's interviews after the White House demanded it (The Hill), and the Washington Examiner reported aides firing back at the press over the firing.
The CNN account rests on anonymous sources, and no post-election firings have been reported.
stories.flag: CNN's account of coming firings relies on anonymous aides and describes expectations, not decisions.
facts: Zacharia was press secretary for about five days.
NBC reports she did not pass her bar exam despite describing herself as a lawyer.
CNN reports aides expect personnel changes if the GOP loses badly Nov. 3.
Trump said there is zero chance he replaces Wiles.
Politico corrected its report on Wiles's role in the Zacharia interviews.
The White House calls the CNN reporting baseless speculation.
stories.left: Critics see an administration that hires without vetting and punishes staff when the polls turn. A press secretary gone in five days, leaks from aides who fear being blamed and talk of a post-election purge suggest a White House that runs on loyalty tests. Democrats argue that voters should weigh how a second-term team behaves under pressure before they hand it two more years with a friendly Congress.
stories.right: Defenders say staff turnover after a rough rollout is normal in any White House and that anonymous-source stories about doom are the media's favorite genre. They point out that Politico had to correct its Wiles reporting and that the White House has denied the purge talk on the record. Conservative commentators add that Trump has stood publicly by Wiles and that midterm blame games are speculation until the votes are counted.
stories.next: Watch for a naming of a new press secretary and for personnel news after Nov. 3.

stories.title: Two weeks out, polls favor Democrats nationally while the Senate stays contested
stories.summary: Fox's poll has Trump at a record-low 36 percent and Democrats up nine on the House ballot, while analysts see a tight Senate.
story: Less than two weeks before Nov. 3, the national numbers lean toward Democrats. The latest Fox News poll, fielded Oct. 9-12 and released Oct. 14, puts Trump's job approval at 36 percent, his lowest in any Fox survey of either term, and has Democrats ahead 54 to 45 on the generic House ballot (Fox News). Fox's Republican pollster Daron Shaw noted some Democratic support sits in lopsided districts, which pads national totals without adding seats.

Trump is campaigning in Kentucky, Kansas, Georgia, South Carolina and Iowa and says he plans to spend more than $400 million to help Republicans, without saying where the money comes from (Fox News). He frames the vote as a referendum on his agenda. Republican voters are frustrated by inflation, gas prices and the Iran war, according to the Fox live coverage. Speaker Mike Johnson says the GOP keeps the House, while Hakeem Jeffries says Democrats have momentum.

The Senate is closer. Republicans hold it 53-47, so Democrats need a net gain of four. National Review's October analysis says Republicans are gaining in Maine, Alaska and Minnesota while facing tougher races in Iowa, Ohio, Kansas and Nebraska. CNN reports Trump's own aides think the House is likely lost but the Senate is holdable.
Polls in individual races are scattered and some are weeks old, so the Senate picture is less certain than the national numbers.
facts: Fox News poll: Trump approval 36 percent, a record low in its surveys.
Fox poll: Democrats lead the generic House ballot 54 to 45.
Republicans hold the Senate 53-47; Democrats need a net gain of four.
Trump says he will spend more than $400 million to help Republicans.
National Review sees GOP gains in Maine, Alaska and Minnesota and tougher races elsewhere.
stories.left: Progressives read the Fox poll as confirmation that inflation, the Iran war and the president's behavior have soured the middle, and they argue Democrats should keep the focus on costs and on checks against an unconstrained White House. They warn that national leads can hide the Senate's tough map, which is why they stress turnout in Maine, Alaska, Ohio and Iowa rather than trusting the topline.
stories.right: Conservatives argue that midterm polls have overstated Democrats before, that a lead built in safe blue districts will not flip many seats and that Senate candidates run on their own records. National Review's case is that Republicans are gaining in several key states and that the party only needs to hold a handful of competitive races. They add that Trump's rallies and his $400 million pledge can still move turnout.
stories.next: Early in-person voting in Alameda County begins Oct. 24, and Election Day is Nov. 3.

stories.title: California fights a federal bid to set aside ballots from 20,000 flagged voters
stories.summary: State officials refuse the Justice Department's demand while a federal court weighs an emergency request.
story: California and Los Angeles County are fighting a Justice Department lawsuit that asks a federal court in the Central District of California to stop the state from tabulating mail ballots from about 20,000 people the department says are likely noncitizens (CalMatters, SF Chronicle). The department filed an emergency motion for a temporary restraining order. Secretary of State Shirley Weber refused to set the ballots aside, writing that she would not disenfranchise Californians "based on an unsupported and likely inaccurate belief" about citizenship.

Attorney General Rob Bonta filed in court urging the judge not to issue the order, and Governor Gavin Newsom called the suit "a sad, desperate attempt" to suppress voters (Fox News, CalMatters). In declarations, Los Angeles County officials said a sample of 200 names from the federal list appeared to be citizens and that most had not voted. The federal count has shrunk from 190,000 flagged by DHS over the summer to the 20,000 in the suit, according to CalMatters.

Federal prosecutor Essayli said the list came from a federal cross-check of voter records with immigration data and that the county's sample figures are meaningless without a way to verify citizenship (Fox News). Prosecutors have charged 28 green card holders from the list, and most cast unlawful ballots, officials said (Washington Examiner).
No ruling on the restraining order had been reported.
stories.flag: No ruling on the emergency motion had been reported at the time of writing.
facts: DOJ wants California barred from tabulating mail ballots from about 20,000 flagged voters.
Weber and Bonta refuse to set the ballots aside.
DHS's summer figure of 190,000 has fallen to 20,000.
An LA County sample of 200 names appeared to be citizens, officials said.
Prosecutors have charged 28 green card holders.
Early voting in Alameda County begins Oct. 24.
stories.left: Democrats and state officials say the case is an election-season attempt to cast doubt on a trusted process. They stress how small the proven number is against 23 million registered voters, how the federal list has shrunk and how Nevada's flagged voters turned out to be citizens. Ordering counties to set ballots aside on unverified data, they argue, risks disenfranchising eligible people who did nothing wrong.
stories.right: Conservatives say federal law bars noncitizens from voting and that California has refused even to review a list compiled by federal agencies. They cite the 28 charged green card holders as evidence that illegal voting happens, and argue that checking the list costs little compared with letting unlawful ballots enter the count. In this view, the state's refusal is the political move.
stories.next: Watch for the judge's decision on the restraining order, which could land before ballots are counted.

stories.title: US and Israel reportedly plan new Iran strikes after the midterms as Hormuz tankers burn
stories.summary: Reports of post-election strike plans pushed Brent to $113 as Iran says seven tankers were hit in the strait.
story: The U.S. and Israel are planning for a possible attack on Iran after the Nov. 3 midterms, NPR reported Thursday, following a New York Times report that the two militaries drafted specific plans for a "short but intensive" operation (NPR, CNBC). Fox News, summarizing the Times, says potential targets include energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities and missile and drone arsenals. CNBC reported Trump told reporters late Wednesday that Washington is not negotiating with Tehran and that something will happen "fairly soon."

Iran said seven oil tankers were targeted in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, with four catching fire and three hitting naval mines (NPR, NBC News). Iran's Revolutionary Guard warned that Gulf data centers and undersea internet cables could be targeted if the U.S. and Israel resume attacks, NPR reported. CNN notes Iran has not said it will sabotage the cables.

The U.S. also ordered non-emergency government employees and families out of Saudi Arabia because of Houthi attacks, the State Department said (CNN, CNBC). A Houthi strike on Riyadh's airport earlier this month killed at least 13 people, CNN reported. At least nine tankers and cargo ships have been attacked since Sunday, CNBC said. Brent crude rose about 4 percent to $113.17, its highest since May 4.
Trump wrote on Oct. 8 that the U.S. would not attack Iran before the midterms, according to a Washington Examiner column. A Washington Examiner column argues the time for a deal is running out.
stories.flag: The Times report rests on unnamed U.S. officials; NPR and CNBC describe it secondhand.
facts: NPR says the U.S. and Israel are planning for a possible attack after Nov. 3.
Iran says seven tankers were hit in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday.
The U.S. ordered non-emergency staff and families out of Saudi Arabia.
Brent crude rose about 4 percent to $113.17, per CNBC.
Iran's Guard threatens Gulf data centers and cables if attacks resume.
stories.left: Progressives argue that planning a strike for the day after an election shows the war is being managed for politics, and that the shipping attacks and Saudi evacuations are the cost of a conflict with no clear end. They want Congress to demand a vote and say the administration should pursue a negotiated deal, not another round of bombing that risks Gulf data centers and a deeper oil shock.
stories.right: Conservatives argue that Iran, not Washington, is escalating by mining and attacking shipping, and that planning ahead is what a serious military does. Writers in the Washington Examiner say the real risk is Trump waiting too long and letting Tehran rebuild, while a deal on uranium and Hormuz remains the better outcome if Iran will accept it. They see the post-election timing as sequencing, not secrecy.
stories.next: Watch for any move on a Hormuz or uranium deal before Nov. 3 and for oil prices at Monday's open.

stories.title: Putin agrees in principle to resume three-way talks as Russia pounds Kyiv
stories.summary: Kremlin aide says talks could come around Nov. 10, and Russia freed an American prisoner.
story: Vladimir Putin told Trump envoy Steve Witkoff on Oct. 21 that he is ready to resume direct peace talks, Axios reported. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said trilateral talks with the U.S. and Ukraine could take place around Nov. 10 in Abu Dhabi, though the dates differ slightly across accounts. Before the meeting, Russia released U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard, 74, who had spent more than four years in prison (NPR, NBC News).

Witkoff had met Volodymyr Zelensky and European leaders in Oslo on Oct. 20 to build a unified "framework agreement," and a U.S. official called progress meaningful (Axios). Ushakov said the Oslo talks "didn't contain much that was useful" (Axios), and the Kremlin said the American nuances do not fully satisfy it. Hours after Russia agreed to the talks, it hit Kyiv with missiles and drones (NBC News).

The U.S.-Ukraine relationship is strained over sanctions relief for Russia. Trump waived sanctions in the Graham Act and defends it as a way to keep Moscow at the table (The Hill). Several Republicans, including Sens. Thom Tillis and John Cornyn, and Rep. Don Bacon, criticized the waiver. Kyiv has accused Washington of withdrawing defense support, which Secretary of State Marco Rubio called "scandalous."
Putin has said any meeting with Zelensky could happen only after a deal is finalized and in Moscow, which Ukraine rejects (Axios).
stories.flag: Accounts differ on the exact timing of the proposed talks.
facts: Putin agreed in principle to resume trilateral talks, per Axios.
Ushakov floated talks around Nov. 10 in Abu Dhabi.
Russia freed American Stephen Hubbard, 74.
Russia struck Kyiv with missiles and drones hours after agreeing.
Trump waived Graham Act sanctions; some Republicans object.
Putin wants any Zelensky meeting only after a deal, in Moscow.
stories.left: Progressives argue that sanctions relief and a diesel deal reward Moscow before it concedes anything, and that the Kremlin uses talks to buy time while striking Kyiv. They want the sanctions Congress passed to take effect and see the Hubbard release as a small gesture that does not change Russia's demands for more land and limits on Ukraine's forces.
stories.right: Conservatives split. Hawks like Tillis and Cornyn say the waiver weakens pressure and betrays allies. Administration allies, including Speaker Mike Johnson, call it the right decision to keep Putin negotiating, and some on the right argue that Washington should stop funding a stalemate and push both sides to a settlement. Commentators in the Washington Examiner criticize Witkoff for praising Putin.
stories.next: Watch for confirmation of the Abu Dhabi date near Nov. 10 and for any congressional move on the sanctions waiver.

stories.title: Oil jumps and Treasury yields dip below 5 percent as jobless claims stay near record lows
stories.summary: Brent hit its highest since May while the 10-year yield fell to 4.95 percent and weekly claims came in at 194,000.
story: Brent crude rose about 4 percent to $113.17 on Thursday, its highest level since May 4, after reports that the U.S. and Israel are weighing renewed strikes on Iran and as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia widened (CNBC). Per CNBC, the 10-year Treasury yield fell below 5 percent for the first time since Sept. 23 as investors sought safe havens during the stock selloff. Market data put the yield at 4.95 percent.

The Labor Department said initial jobless claims fell to 194,000 for the week ended Oct. 17, below the roughly 200,000 economists expected and near the lowest since the 1960s (CNBC). CNBC called it a low-hire, low-fire market. September payrolls rose only 29,000 and unemployment ticked up to 4.2 percent (CNBC). Housing starts came in at 1.22 million against 1.3 million expected, and homebuilder sentiment is at a 14-year low.

Inflation is the Federal Reserve's problem. September CPI rose 3.7 percent from a year earlier, up from 3.4 percent, while core CPI was 2.6 percent (Fox Business, CNBC). The Fed meets Oct. 27-28, and the consensus is a hold with a December hike in play (CNBC).
For households, the mix is gasoline pressure and a frozen housing market, even as layoffs stay rare.
stories.flag: Reports differ on WTI's daily change, so it is left out.
facts: Brent rose about 4 percent to $113.17, the highest since May 4.
The 10-year Treasury yield is 4.95 percent, below 5 percent for the first time since Sept. 23.
Jobless claims were 194,000 for the week ended Oct. 17.
Housing starts were 1.22 million versus 1.3 million expected.
September CPI was 3.7 percent year over year.
The Fed meets Oct. 27-28.
stories.left: Progressives see a labor market with little hiring and housing that few can afford, and they say costs rather than layoffs are what households feel. They argue energy shocks from the Iran war and immigration limits that shrink construction labor and rising material costs fall on workers and first-time buyers, and that the Fed should not add pain with more hikes.
stories.right: Conservatives point to the record-low layoffs as evidence that the economy is sturdier than the headlines suggest and blame inflation on energy prices and past spending. Many argue the Fed must hold its 2 percent target, as Fed leader Kevin Warsh has said, and that a deal that reopens Hormuz would do more to cut prices than any rate move.

stories.title: Nasdaq falls 2.6 percent, its worst day since June, as AI funding fears meet an oil spike
stories.summary: Chip and AI infrastructure names led the drop while the Dow edged up on a bond rally.
story: The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.60 percent to 26,008.86 on Thursday, its worst day since June, and the S&P 500 lost 1.21 percent to 7,663.43. The Dow rose 0.02 percent to 52,867.98 as investors rotated into defensive and dividend stocks (CNBC). Bloomberg reported the Nasdaq 100 down about 2.9 percent and the Philadelphia semiconductor index down 6.7 percent at their worst intraday.

The causes were worry about how the AI buildout will be paid for and a jump in oil. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC neocloud demand is "off the charts" but capital is scarce. CNBC reported Nvidia fell 4.4 percent, Alphabet 3.2 percent, AMD 8.1 percent, CoreWeave 10 percent and Micron 6 percent. Meta fell about 7 percent despite a revenue beat (CNBC).

A bond rally cushioned some sectors, with the 10-year yield below 5 percent. Analyst Dan Ives argued AI computing demand remains robust (CNBC). NBC News tied the move to the collision of Iran war worries and AI spending doubts.
Of your watchlist, Amazon fell 4.57 percent, Nvidia 4.40 percent, Alphabet 3.15 percent, Tesla 3.08 percent and Microsoft 2.23 percent, while Apple rose 1.23 percent.
facts: Nasdaq fell 2.60 percent to 26,008.86, its worst day since June.
S&P 500 fell 1.21 percent to 7,663.43.
The Dow rose 0.02 percent to 52,867.98.
Nvidia fell 4.4 percent and AMD 8.1 percent, per CNBC.
Alphabet and Microsoft report Oct. 28 after the close; Amazon reports Oct. 29.
stories.why: Investors are asking who will fund the AI data center boom, and Huang's own words about scarce capital sharpened the worry. Higher oil and yields near 5 percent raise financing costs. That matters for your watchlist because Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon report earnings in the next week, where capital spending plans will be scrutinized.
stories.next: Alphabet and Microsoft report Oct. 28 after the close and Amazon follows Oct. 29, with the Fed deciding Oct. 28.

stories.title: IBM spin-off Anderon builds a quantum chip foundry on a 300mm line in Albany
stories.summary: A finalized $1 billion CHIPS award and IBM's matching $1 billion back a foundry for quantum hardware, but customers beyond IBM are still unproven.
story: Anderon, a quantum chip foundry IBM set up this year, has a finalized Commerce Department R&D award of up to $1 billion, announced Sept. 16, with IBM adding a matching $1 billion plus intellectual property, assets and staff (IEEE Spectrum). The company is led by former semiconductor executive Mukesh Khare. Its first wafers are already running on a 300mm production line in Albany, New York.

The idea is to run quantum hardware like a conventional silicon foundry, so designers can focus on chips instead of building their own fabs (IEEE Spectrum). The line supports superconducting qubit wafers and related electronics, with plans to expand to other architectures later (Constellation Research). Commerce also finalized up to $375 million for GlobalFoundries and up to $100 million each for Rigetti, D-Wave, Quantinuum and PsiQuantum, per Spectrum. Total federal and private funding is roughly $2 billion, though sources differ slightly on the total.

The risk is demand. Futurum Group argues the question now moves from funding to whether a customer base beyond IBM appears for specialized quantum wafers. IEEE Spectrum adds that extending the foundry to trapped-ion or photonic qubits would need process development Anderon has not detailed publicly.
A foundry model would let several quantum companies share tooling and yield learning, the way classical chip designers do with TSMC.
facts: The Commerce award of up to $1 billion was finalized Sept. 16.
IBM is adding $1 billion of its own.
The fab is a 300mm line in Albany, N.Y.
It targets superconducting qubit wafers first.
Commerce also awarded $375 million to GlobalFoundries and $100 million each to four quantum firms.
stories.why: Quantum processors are still built in small in-house fabs, which limits how fast designs can iterate. A shared 300mm line could standardize processes and lower costs. Whether it works depends on winning customers other than IBM and on adapting the line to other qubit types.
stories.next: Watch for the first outside customer announcement and for wafer yield data.

stories.title: EU steel safeguards on transformer cores split steelmakers and grid builders
stories.summary: Temporary import price floors on electrical steel aim to protect two EU mills, but transformer makers warn of higher grid costs.
story: The European Commission has put temporary safeguards on imports of grain-oriented electrical steel, the material in transformer cores, running from late September to Feb. 26, 2027 (GMK Center). The measures use import quotas with price floors, which range from 2,800 to 3,400 euros per metric ton within quotas and rise to 3,500 euros once a quota is filled. Shipments priced below the floor owe a duty equal to the gap. The rules also cover laminations, cores and cores already fitted in imported transformers.

The Commission says EU producers' market share fell from 66 percent in 2021 to 43 percent in 2025 despite rising demand, with global overcapacity redirecting steel to Europe (GMK Center). Thyssenkrupp Electrical Steel says EU imports have tripled since 2022 and rose another 50 percent in 2025, and it shut its Isbergues plant in France from June to September and cut output at Gelsenkirchen in Germany (Steel Technology).

Transformer makers object. T&D Europe's Diederik Peereboom argues the measure shifts more than 700 million euros a year from the transformer industry to just two EU producers of the steel, Thyssenkrupp and Stalprodukt (GMK Center, IEEE Spectrum). The electrical industry group ZVEI says imports from partners such as Japan and South Korea will stay essential until European mills scale up, and critics fear manufacturers may move transformer production out of Europe (IEEE Spectrum).

Transformer supply is already tight as AI data centers and electrification pull on the grid, so the price of the steel feeds directly into grid build-out costs. The Commission decides by February whether to make the safeguards longer term.
stories.flag: The 700 million euro cost figure comes from industry group T&D Europe, not the Commission.
facts: Safeguards run from late September 2026 to Feb. 26, 2027.
Price floors range from 2,800 to 3,500 euros per metric ton depending on quota.
EU producers' market share fell from 66 percent to 43 percent between 2021 and 2025.
Only two EU steelmakers, Thyssenkrupp and Stalprodukt, make the steel.
T&D Europe claims a transfer of more than 700 million euros a year.
stories.why: Grain-oriented electrical steel sets the efficiency and supply of power transformers, one of the slowest-to-build parts of the grid. Protecting local mills could secure a European source, while higher prices could slow new lines and data center hookups. The February review will decide which risk the EU accepts.
stories.next: Watch for the Commission's decision before the safeguards expire on Feb. 26, 2027.

stories.title: Modeling study says Earth and Mars were built in different ways
stories.summary: University of Copenhagen researchers find Earth grew mostly from pebbles and Mars from larger planetesimals, though the result rests on model assumptions.
story: A University of Copenhagen team reports that Earth and Mars formed through different processes even though they came from the same region of the early solar system (Space.com). The study was published in Nature Astronomy in early October. The researchers examined volatile elements such as sodium, zinc and potassium in the crust and mantle of each planet to infer how they were assembled.

Their modeling suggests at least 75 percent of Earth's mass came from protoplanets that grew by accreting pebbles, with planetesimals supplying up to 25 percent. For Mars, roughly three-quarters came from planetesimals and the rest from pebble accretion (Space.com). The results support a hybrid picture in which both pebble accretion and planetesimal collisions shaped the rocky planets.

The authors stress the results depend on modeling assumptions. They treat the planetesimal building blocks of both planets as chemically similar to the asteroid Vesta and assume volatiles are lost more efficiently during pebble accretion than in giant impacts (Space.com). Coverage by Universe Today and Astrobiology.com describes the same finding.
If the model holds, it explains why Mars ended up smaller and chemically distinct without needing different source regions.
stories.flag: The result is model-dependent; the authors list the Vesta-like composition and volatile-loss assumptions as caveats.
facts: The study is from the University of Copenhagen, published in Nature Astronomy.
Earth drew at least 75 percent of its mass from pebble-grown protoplanets in the model.
Mars drew roughly 75 percent from planetesimals.
The work relies on volatile elements such as sodium, zinc and potassium.
Assumptions include Vesta-like planetesimals.
stories.why: How rocky planets assemble determines their composition, water content and habitability. A split in building methods would mean neighbors in the same disk can end up very different. Samples from Mars and better volatile measurements could test it.
stories.next: Watch for rebuttals or tests using Mars sample data and new volatile measurements.

stories.title: Tooth enamel shows Peak District children were poisoned by lead from the seventh century
stories.summary: A study in Antiquity finds the medieval lead industry exposed poorer households far more than elites.
story: Researchers led by the University of Nottingham used chemical traces in tooth enamel to reconstruct centuries of lead exposure in the Peak District, finding the industry had restarted by the middle of the seventh century and was affecting the environment at scale by the eighth (University of Nottingham, ITV News). The work appeared in the journal Antiquity, with the British Geological Survey, the University of Sheffield, York Archaeology and the Castleton Historical Society.

Tooth enamel forms in childhood and does not remodel, so it keeps a permanent record of lead absorbed early in life (Popular Science). The teeth came from three Peak District cemeteries dating between 650 and 1500 CE. Lead levels in Derbyshire mining communities in the seventh century matched or exceeded those in industrial cities of the 1700s and 1800s, the researchers report.

People buried with high-status grave goods, including weapons, generally had much lower lead levels than those from less richly furnished graves. The authors suggest elites controlled or profited from lead production while lower-status households did the ore processing and smelting, exposing their children to far more pollution. They also flag possible vulnerability among women and raise, without proving, that exposure contributed to premature deaths of women of childbearing age (University of Nottingham).
Most coverage rewrites the university release, so details should be checked against the paper.
stories.flag: Links between exposure and early deaths are a hypothesis raised by the authors, not an established finding.
facts: The study was published in Antiquity and led by the University of Nottingham.
Teeth came from three cemeteries dated 650 to 1500 CE.
Lead production had restarted by the mid-seventh century.
Elite burials had lower lead levels than poorer burials.
Seventh-century exposure matched industrial cities of the 1700s and 1800s.
stories.why: The study shows that environmental pollution and inequality were linked more than a thousand years ago, and gives archaeologists a way to date industrial activity from skeletons. It also shows how long lead contamination can leave a mark on communities.
stories.next: Watch for follow-up isotope work on other medieval mining regions.

stories.title: Nvidia's Huang says neocloud demand is huge but capital is scarce, and markets flinch
stories.summary: Comments at GTC Berlin helped drag CoreWeave down 10 percent as investors question how AI data centers get financed.
story: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said Thursday at the company's GTC conference in Berlin that neocloud demand is "off the charts" but capital is scarce, describing a gap in which "the demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital" (CNBC). He said the gap will get solved. Bloomberg video separately quoted him calling neoclouds a good investment.

Markets did not take it calmly. CoreWeave fell about 10 percent and Wells Fargo traders said his remarks were spooking markets, according to CNBC. The Nasdaq fell 2.6 percent that day. Huang also told CNBC he sees no sign of a memory glut by 2029 and that "you can always use more" memory, after a recent selloff in memory stocks.

Axios notes investors are scrutinizing a circular flow in which Nvidia helps finance companies that buy its chips. Nvidia took a $2 billion stake in CoreWeave in January and has put more than $40 billion into equity bets this year, CNBC reported earlier. Nvidia has also taken stakes in startups in Britain and France during this European tour.
The message underlines that the AI boom now depends as much on credit markets and borrowing costs as on chips.
facts: Huang spoke at GTC Berlin on Oct. 22.
He said neocloud demand is off the charts but capital is scarce.
CoreWeave fell about 10 percent that day, per CNBC.
Huang sees no sign of a memory glut by 2029.
Nvidia invested $2 billion in CoreWeave in January.
stories.why: Neoclouds borrow heavily to buy GPUs, so scarce capital slows chip orders and raises the risk of defaults if demand lags. If Huang is right that demand is strong, the bottleneck is financing, which makes interest rates and credit appetite as important to AI as model quality.
stories.next: Watch Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon earnings Oct. 28 and 29 for capital spending guidance, and for neocloud financing deals.

stories.title: OpenAI widens its Decisions API, a rival to TypeSafe's Jev for supervising AI agents
stories.summary: The model returns choices, scores or probabilities instead of text, at $0.10 per million input tokens.
story: OpenAI made its Decisions API broadly available to developers, TechCrunch reported Thursday, as competition grows over so-called decision models that supervise AI agents. Other accounts say it opened in public beta on Oct. 6 after a limited preview at DevDay, so the exact status differs by source (Dealroom, TechCrunch).

The API runs on GPT-6 Luna, currently the only supported model. Instead of generating text, it returns a probability that a statement is true, a choice from a fixed set with confidence scores, or a score (Firecrawl, Dealroom). It accepts text and images. Dealroom lists pricing of $0.10 per million input tokens with no output-token charge, and OpenAI claims it is up to 10 times faster than calling Luna through the Responses API, a comparison Firecrawl notes is against Luna itself.

TypeSafe AI's Jev, the model OpenAI is chasing, lists at $0.042 per million input tokens and is text-only, per Firecrawl. Amazon released its own open-weight decision model, Strands Decider 2B, and Cloudflare followed with Clef (TechCrunch). OpenAI is keeping its model behind a hosted API.
TechCrunch reports OpenAI's model sits eighth and fourteenth on two decision-model indices, behind Jev and others.
stories.flag: Sources conflict on whether the API is in public beta or generally available.
facts: OpenAI's Decisions API runs on GPT-6 Luna.
It returns predicates, choices or scores rather than text.
Dealroom lists $0.10 per million input tokens.
Jev lists at $0.042 per million input tokens and is text-only.
Amazon and Cloudflare have released rival decision models.
stories.why: Small, fast models that grade or route an agent's actions are becoming the control layer for agentic systems. Cheap per-call scoring makes it practical to check every step, and the price war suggests the layer may commoditize quickly.
stories.next: Watch for general availability and for independent benchmark results on the decision-model indices.

stories.title: Trump says data centers should pay host communities a dividend
stories.summary: The idea comes as local opposition to data centers splits Republicans ahead of the midterms.
story: President Trump posted on Truth Social that data center operators should pay a dividend to the communities and people near their facilities to win local support, and argued his mandate for large sites to generate their own power could lower prices (CNBC, Fox News). No formal program or funding mechanism was announced. An executive at Nebius told CNBC the idea is "not crazy."

The proposal builds on the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, a voluntary commitment by seven major AI developers to cover the cost of added electricity production. Fox News reports the pledge has expanded to 23 governors and about 200 stakeholders. CNBC says residential electricity prices rose 6 percent on average in 2025 despite Trump's promise to cut them in half.

Data centers are a midterm problem. A June Yale poll found 53 percent of conservative Republicans oppose building data centers locally (CNBC). Fox News reports the push has fractured Republicans in Congress, with Rep. Ralph Norman saying decisions should rest with states and localities. Democrats have called the original pledge an empty promise (CNBC).
Experts quoted by CNBC question whether such commitments are credible when hyperscalers still struggle to turn profits.
stories.flag: No details on who would be paid, how much or how it would be enforced.
facts: Trump urged data centers to pay communities a dividend.
No formal program was announced.
Seven AI developers signed the voluntary Ratepayer Protection Pledge.
Residential electricity prices rose 6 percent on average in 2025.
A June Yale poll found 53 percent of conservative Republicans oppose local data centers.
stories.left: Progressives and many local groups say voluntary pledges and dividends do not protect ratepayers. They want binding rules making large power users pay for the grid upgrades they require, plus water and environmental review, and they note that bills already rose. A check to residents, they argue, should not replace enforceable protections.
stories.right: Many conservatives favor letting localities decide and see the dividend as a market-friendly way to share benefits while keeping the build-out in America. Others on the right, including Rep. Ralph Norman, argue data center siting is a state and local matter and that Washington should not push it. They stress self-generated power as a way to avoid raising bills.
stories.next: Watch for any actual dividend terms and for state-level data center moratorium fights.

briefs: France banned planned protests in Paris, Lyon, Lille and Grenoble on Thursday after President Macron called some demonstrations illegitimate, NBC News reported.
An early flu season is hitting the West Coast first, driven by an H1N1 strain with a new mutation that was not in this year's vaccine strain choice; experts urge shots now, CNN reported.
SpaceX stock jumped about 10 percent after an earnings beat and Musk hinted at a Tesla tie-up, CNBC reported Oct. 21.
The Fed meets Oct. 27-28, and CNBC's analysis says a hold is the consensus, with a December hike seen as more likely.
